title: Bright red, in the basin
objective: Explain how portal hypertension causes varices, ascites and hepatorenal syndrome, and support the patient through variceal bleeding treatment including TIPS
secondaryObjectives: In acute upper GI bleeding, place two large-bore IVs, restore volume and blood pressure, protect the airway in massive hematemesis, and read a high BUN-to-creatinine ratio as a clue to an upper source

brief.situation: 03:00 in a medical ICU. You are Mr. Reyes's nurse. He is 56, with alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites, admitted yesterday with mild hepatic encephalopathy. He has just vomited about 400 mL of bright red blood.
handover: Access: one 22-gauge IV in his hand. Yesterday's hemoglobin 9.8, platelets 72, INR 1.9.
He is drowsy but rousable. The intensivist is in the unit; the GI team is on call for endoscopy.

Unit policy for suspected variceal bleeding: airway first (on his side, suction, anesthesia if he cannot protect it), two large-bore IVs and a crossmatch, the ordered vasoactive drug and antibiotic as soon as ordered, transfusion to the ordered hemoglobin goal.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Where is this blood coming from, why, and what does he need in what order?

parts.label: Where and why
parts.criteria: Portal hypertension from cirrhosis (ascites, caput medusae, splenomegaly) causes varices; hematemesis with a high BUN-to-creatinine ratio fits an upper source; suspected variceal hemorrhage.
parts.modelAnswer: Cirrhosis raises the pressure in the portal system, so blood backs up into varices in the esophagus; the ascites and caput medusae are the same pressure. Bright red hematemesis and a high BUN-to-creatinine ratio point to an upper source. This is a variceal bleed until proved otherwise.

parts.label: In what order
parts.criteria: Airway first (side, suction, anesthesia); two large-bore IVs; the vasoactive drug as soon as suspected and the antibiotic; restrictive transfusion to a hemoglobin of 7 to 9, not above; urgent endoscopy within 12 hours; TIPS if bleeding cannot be controlled.
parts.modelAnswer: Protect his airway first, then two large-bore IVs. Call now for octreotide and an antibiotic, and blood to a hemoglobin of 7 to 9, not higher, because over-transfusing raises portal pressure. Then endoscopy for banding, and TIPS if the bleeding can't be controlled.

Suspected variceal bleed. Call the intensivist; two large-bore IVs; stat labs and crossmatch.
Octreotide and the antibiotic as soon as ordered; red cells to a hemoglobin of 7 to 9.
Document; anesthesia intubates; GI bands; TIPS if it fails.

shock.headline: Shock and aspiration
shock.body: Hematemesis in cirrhosis is variceal until proved otherwise: airway, access, a vasoactive drug as soon as suspected, an antibiotic, restrictive transfusion and urgent endoscopy.

toScope.headline: Stabilized for endoscopy
toScope.body: You protected his airway, got access, called within minutes, started octreotide and the antibiotic and transfused to the goal. That is the expert path.

toScopeGaps.headline: To endoscopy, with gaps
toScopeGaps.body: Check the time to octreotide, whether his airway and access were secured, whether the antibiotic went in and whether he was over-transfused.

time_up.headline: Still bleeding
time_up.body: A vasoactive drug starts as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected.

scoring.modelReasoning: Cirrhosis raises portal pressure, which opens varices and drives ascites (and, in the kidney, hepatorenal syndrome). Bright red hematemesis with a high BUN-to-creatinine ratio in a man with ascites and caput medusae is a variceal bleed until proved otherwise. Protect the airway first, place two large-bore IVs, and call now: a vasoactive drug such as octreotide as soon as it is suspected, a short course of antibiotic, red cells to a hemoglobin of 7 to 9 (not above, because over-transfusion raises portal pressure), endoscopy within 12 hours for banding, and TIPS if bleeding cannot be controlled or recurs.
